title: Continuous batching: scheduler tuning experiments (batch size, timeout, fairness, tail latency)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a sequence of controlled experiments to tune our continuous-batching scheduler. The goal was to quantify how batch_size, scheduling timeout (max wait), and fairness policies impact throughput and tail latency (P95/P99) for mixed workloads. Results informed a set of recommended defaults and an adaptive policy prototype for production.

Motivation / context:
- Continuous batching improves GPU utilization and amortizes per-request overhead, but naive batching can inflate tail latency for small/latency-sensitive requests.
- We need clear tradeoffs for: max_batch_size, max_wait_ms (scheduling timeout), and fairness (how to prefer small/fast requests vs large ones).
- Experiments were run to profile bottlenecks, measure latency distributions, and validate an adaptive timeout that reduces P99 regressions while preserving most throughput gains.

Environment / test harness:
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.14.3 (branch: batching-tuning-experiments).
- Hardware: single-node tests on p4d.24xlarge-equivalent (8xA100-80GB) and scaled runs on cluster w/ 4 nodes (32 GPUs total).
- Model used: opt-30b-8k quantized variant (latency- and memory-representative).
- Workloads: synthetic mix and replayed production traces (sanitized).
  - Mixed-1: 60% short requests (seq_len <= 128), 30% medium (128-512), 10% long (>512).
  - LATENCY-ONLY: 95% short requests (to study low-latency tail).
  - THROUGHPUT-ONLY: large-batch-friendly long requests.
- Client QPS: scaled to saturate GPU (target 90% utilization for throughput runs); also tested with low QPS to test latency.
- Metrics captured: throughput (tokens/s), request/sec, P50/P90/P95/P99 latency (end-to-end and server-side), GPU utilization, CPU (scheduler) utilization, batch size distribution, #batches formed per second, and queue length.
- Tools: perf/top/ttop for kernel profiling, eBPF traces for scheduler hotpaths, server profiling enabled (sampling), and a light-weight in-runtime tracepoint for batch-formation timing.

Experiment matrix:
- max_batch_size: [8, 16, 32, 64]
- max_wait_ms: [1, 5, 10, 25, 50]
- fairness policies: [FIFO, size-aware-weighted, priority-small-first]
- For each combination: run Mixed-1 at target QPS and record 30-minute steady-state window.

Key findings (high-level):
1) Throughput vs max_batch_size:
   - Throughput (tokens/s) increases with max_batch_size up to 32, with diminishing returns beyond 32 for our model/hardware. 64 yields ~3% extra throughput vs 32 but increased P99 for latency-sensitive requests.
2) Timeout effects (max_wait_ms):
   - Very small timeouts (1ms) reduce formed batch sizes and give best P50/P90 but hurt throughput significantly (~20-30% lower than 10ms/25ms).
   - Longer timeouts (25-50ms) raise P95/P99 strongly for short requests when mixed with long requests; tail latency spikes are caused by long requests blocking batch formation or inflating batch service time.
3) Fairness policies:
   - FIFO favors earlier arrivals and can starve short latency-sensitive requests when large requests arrive concurrently.
   - Size-aware-weighted policy (weights inversely proportional to sequence length) significantly reduces P99 for short requests with only modest through-put cost (~5%).
   - Priority-small-first policy (strict priority) minimizes tail latency for short requests but causes noticeable throughput drop for long-request-dominated workloads and can increase latency variance for those long requests.

Profiling / bottlenecks observed:
- Scheduler CPU usage: When max_wait_ms is low (1-5ms), the scheduler became CPU-bound due to more frequent wakeups and smaller batches. eBPF traces show hot loops in queue scanning and lock contention around per-priority queues.
- Batch formation latency: median formation time was ~1.2ms for batch_size target 32, but P99 formation time moved to ~35ms when long requests queued and blocked some worker pools.
- GPU utilization: batch-size increases improved GPU occupancy up to ~70-75%; beyond that kernel launch overheads and memory constraints reduced incremental gains.
- KV-cache behavior: For longer requests hitting KV-cache misses, service time variance increased and padded tails.

Representative numbers (Mixed-1, single-node, opt-30b):
- Baseline (max_batch_size=16, max_wait_ms=10, FIFO): throughput=120k tokens/s, P50=40ms, P95=220ms, P99=480ms.
- Tuned (max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=10, size-aware-weighted): throughput=145k tokens/s, P50=42ms, P95=180ms, P99=230ms.
- Low-latency config (max_batch_size=16, max_wait_ms=1, priority-small-first): throughput=100k tokens/s, P50=28ms, P95=95ms, P99=130ms.

Observations / interpretation:
- A modest max_batch_size (32) with a medium timeout (~10ms) is a good throughput/latency sweet spot for mixed workloads on this hardware and model. It gives sizeable throughput gains over 16 without large P99 regressions when paired with a fairness policy.
- Fairness matters: the size-aware-weighted scheduler reduced P99 by ~2x in mixed scenarios while preserving most throughput. The scheduling overhead of the weighted policy was small relative to overall scheduling cost and can be optimized (see code-level hotpath notes).
- Very aggressive low wait times (<=1ms) help latency-sensitive SLAs but at non-trivial throughput cost. These are appropriate for dedicated low-latency tiers rather than default hosted workloads.

Code/config snippets used (examples):
- Scheduler config (YAML-like pseudo):
  scheduler:
    max_batch_size: 32
    max_wait_ms: 10
    fairness: size_aware_weighted
    weight_fn: "inverse_length"  # weight ~ 1/seq_len (clamped)
    priority_buckets: [small, medium, large]

- Perf command examples:
  - Run steady trace (30min) with tracepoints: ./run_bench --tracepoint scheduler:batch_formed --duration 1800 --workload mixed-1
  - eBPF queue trace: sudo ./ebpf_queue_trace -p <server_pid> --duration 300

Runtime micro-optimizations discovered:
- Reduce lock hold time when scanning per-bucket queues: swap pointers to a local buffer under lock and process unlocked. Reduced scheduler CPU by ~18% under heavy small-request load.
- Inline quick-path for single-request batch (when only one request in run-loop) to avoid constructing batch metadata for trivial batches.
- Compact weight calculation: precompute / clamp weights in small lookup table to avoid expensive floating divide in scheduler hotpath. Saved ~6% CPU.

Risk / failure modes:
- Strict priority for small requests can cause starvation for throughput-focused customers; must be opt-in or used only for dedicated low-latency pools.
- Adaptive policies that reduce timeout when load is low must ensure oscillation doesn't occur (hysteresis needed).

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Default config for hosted mixed workloads: max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=10, fairness=size_aware_weighted, weight_fn=inverse_length (clamped to [0.2,1.0]).
2) Add an explicit low-latency tier config: max_batch_size=16, max_wait_ms=1, strict_small_priority=true; intended for dedicated latency-sensitive routes.
3) Implement adaptive timeout prototype: target_wait_ms = min( configured_max_wait, latency_budget_based_on_queue_depth ), with simple hysteresis (5% / 200ms window) to avoid oscillation.
4) Fix scheduler hotpaths from profiling (PR in flight: linked_artifacts PR #782) and add micro-optimizations noted above.
5) Add automated benchmarks to CI that replay representative mixed traces and assert P95/P99 bounds for default config.

Next steps / open questions:
- Validate results across other model families (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder) and smaller/larger model sizes. We expect tuning numbers to vary; constrained devices may prefer smaller max_batch_size.
- Explore hybrid batching: allow small requests to be dispatched in separate fast-path pools that periodically flush to large batches for throughput (e.g., 80% small-only pool + periodic merge).
- Evaluate fairness with real production traffic (A/B test) to measure user-perceived latency changes and any regressions to throughput for enterprise customers.
- Flesh out adaptive timeout algorithm and run long-running (24h) tests to surface oscillation or edge cases.

Appendix: raw experiment notes and traces
- See attached traces and summarized CSVs in the experiment folder (internal link): drive:/shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/experiments/continuous-batching/ (artifact upload pending).
- Quick checklist for replicating a run:
  - Checkout branch batching-tuning-experiments
  - Start server with --config scheduler.max_batch_size=32 --config scheduler.max_wait_ms=10 --config scheduler.fairness=size_aware_weighted
  - Run bench harness: ./bench/run --workload mixed-1 --duration 1800 --target_qps <saturating_qps>
  - Capture traces: ./collect_traces.sh <pid> output_dir

If reviewers want, I can fold these results into the Confluence runbook (linked) and prepare a short internal slide deck summarizing the recommended defaults and tradeoffs for the SRE and Product teams.

Author notes: this doc is intentionally pragmatic (many quick measurements and config trials). The next version will include CI-driven dashboards and longer-run stability tests.
